thread.title: Fed Rate-Hike Odds Fall As Dow Jones Slides; Why The Federal Reserve May Punt

author: JED GRAHAM
title: Fed Rate-Hike Odds Fall As Dow Jones Slides; Why The Federal Reserve May Punt

organizations.name: fed rate-hike odds fall as dow jones slides

text:
Financial markets are pricing in just 70% odds of a Fed rate hike on Wednesday after the Dow Jones and broader stock market broke through recent lows on the stock market today . That's a far cry from the near certainty (typically 90%-plus rate-hike odds) that preceded the seven hikes over the past two years. Here are 11 reasons why the Federal Reserve meeting could deliver a surprise, but the first may be the most essential and the stock market seems to be cooperating. The Dow Jones closed off more than 500 points on Monday, while the S&P 500 hit its lowest level of the year and the Nasdaq settled at a 52-week closing low.
X Dow Jones, Major Averages Break Support With the S&P 500 index briefly crashing through 52-week lows hit in the early 2018 stock market correction, further weakness on Tuesday could make the Fed's policy move close to a tossup. The Dow almost made a 52-week low, falling to within 115 points of its low-water mark.
If the Fed's plan is to hurry up (hike rates this week) and wait (signal at least a brief pause to the market to get a clearer sense of where the economy is headed), policymakers may start to ask, "What's the hurry?" There isn't one.
It's one thing to raise rates when markets are in the lower end of a trading range, but another when stocks bust through support and it's unclear how far they'll fall. While the Fed isn't especially concerned about the stock market, there are 10 other reasons why a pause may make sense.

Please contact customer service CLOSE China Slowdown The latest raft of disappointing economic data out of China that hit global financial markets on Friday recalls the Fed's move in December 2015 to press ahead with their first rate hike in a decade. By January, financial markets were tumbling as China's currency wobbled, and policymakers hit the pause button, delaying the next Fed rate hike for a year.
The experience won't be lost on the Fed policymakers meeting on Tuesday and Wednesday. Everything worked out fine last time around as China flooded its economy with stimulus, but that's not something the Fed can count on in 2019.
China Trade War The biggest uncertainty weighing on U.S. businesses, China and the global economy is the potential escalation of the China trade war with new President Trump tariffs that could hit starting March 1. There are good reasons to expect a deal, as China has made a show of responding to U.S. demands, and Trump clearly wants to claim victory.
But there's also risk that the geopolitical rivalry between the U.S. and China could turn into a technological cold war that proves disruptive for the global economy and for companies like Apple ( AAPL ) that depend on China as a major market and a manufacturing base. Apple is reportedly mulling a possible move of iPhone manufacturing from China if it faces 25% Trump tariffs.
The Fed's approach has been to ignore uncertainty until it shows up in the data, yet China trade war risks are a likely factor in the slowing growth of business investment.
Slowing U.S. Economy The U.S. economy has been on a roll, as November retail sales confirmed, but the growth spurt seems to be winding down. Growth is expected to decelerate to about 3% this quarter from 3.5% in Q3 and 4.2% in Q4. While the economy is doing fine, the slowing has broadened out, with business spending joining housing and autos.
Mild Inflation Meanwhile, there's no urgency for a fourth Fed rate hike rates this year with inflation showing no signs of an upsurge. After finally hitting the 2.0% target, the Fed's preferred inflation gauge, the core personal consumption expenditures price index, slipped back to 1.8% in October. Economists expect a 1.9% core inflation reading for November.
The Strong Dollar A number of Fed policymakers have noted slowing global growth as a downside risk to the U.S., and it's hard to ignore the procyclical role of the dollar. A stronger dollar is a negative for the global economy, as money leaves emerging markets to seek shelter in U.S. Treasuries and other dollar-based relatively safe assets. A stronger dollar also dampens profit growth for U.S. multinationals that get much of their revenue in foreign currencies. Further, a strong dollar makes it harder for emerging market economies that rely on dollar-based loans to service their debts. On Friday, the dollar was flirting with its highest level in 18 months.
The Treasury Yield Curve Federal Reserve policymakers have taken the flattening of the Treasury yield curve mostly in stride, but there are exceptions. Atlanta Fed President Raphael Bostic has said the Fed should take care not to willfully invert the Treasury yield curve. That point is getting uncomfortably close, with just 16 basis points between the 2-year and 10-year Treasury yields. The belly of the curve already has inverted, with 2-year Treasury yields higher than 3-year and 5-year yields on Monday.
Junk Bonds Fed Chairman Jerome Powell has hinted that he cares more about corporate bond markets than the Dow Jones. Lately, corporate bond yields are signaling that investors have a lower appetite for risk. The Financial Times noted recently that the spreads between Treasuries and bonds issued by higher-risk companies (those with triple-C ratings or lower) widened by 257 basis points since the end of September.
Federal Reserve Credibility The central bank has earned credibility after seven quarter-point Fed rate hikes since December 2016, while inflation has mostly remained below target. Notably, three of those Fed rate hikes came after the stock market faltered early this year.
Fed Chairman Powell Shift Fed Chairman Powell's big shift last month was really to become a consensus builder. Previously, he emphasized his own view, and perhaps the median view, of where the neutral federal funds rate is. Last month, he highlighted that the Fed's key rate was "just below" the broad range of estimates of the neutral rate, where policy is neither slowing or boosting the economy.
The slide in the Dow Jones and broader stock market likely have only raised the importance of a unanimous vote to raise rates, in Powell's view. If one of a trio of possible dissenters signals a desire to hold off on the next Fed rate hike, that one vote could move the crowd.
Fed Signaling The Fed is anxious to drive home that interest-rate policy going forward will be heavily data dependent. That's a signal to financial markets not to sweat the Fed rate hike projections released this week.
Yet it may occur to policymakers that there's only really one sure way to demonstrate the Fed's patience: Leaving rates unchanged, while saying they expect a gradual pace of rate hikes will be appropriate.
While President Trump made his own case via tweet for the Fed to hold off on rate hikes , Fed policymakers will likely base their decision on the merits, without worry about the appearance of caving to pressure.
